author: Dorothy Brooks
title: Antibodies Against DNA Repair Proteins Appeared Years Before Diagnosis in Some Children Who Later Developed Cancer
text:
Antibodies Against DNA Repair Proteins Appeared Years Before Diagnosis in Some Children Who Later Developed Cancer
Children who were later diagnosed with cancer were more likely to have antibodies in their blood that target the body's own DNA repair proteins, in some cases years before diagnosis, according to researchers at the University of Bergen in Norway. The findings were published Oct. 14 in Frontiers in Immunology.
The work points to a possible early warning sign for cancer in young people. In the United States, an estimated 14,910 children and adolescents ages 0 to 19 were expected to be diagnosed with cancer in 2024, according to the National Cancer Institute's childhood cancer fact sheet.
This is not a test parents can use today. The study found an association, not proof that these antibodies cause cancer, and the key early-warning analysis included only 30 people who later developed cancer.
Antibodies That Target the Body's Repair System
Antibodies normally fight germs. Autoantibodies are different because they mistakenly target the body's own proteins. In this study, the researchers looked for autoantibodies aimed at proteins that repair damaged DNA, part of the cell's system for fixing errors before they become harmful mutations.
The team first compared blood from 175 children and adults with nine cancer types, including several sarcomas and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, with blood from 141 healthy people. The patient samples came from Norwegian studies and biobanks, including the Norwegian Childhood Cancer Biobank. Children with cancer had more antibodies against several DNA repair proteins, including RAD52, UNG, and MGMT, Newsweek reported.
To see whether the antibodies appeared before cancer, the team examined stored blood from two long-running British child health studies, the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children and Born in Bradford. The researchers compared 30 people who gave blood as healthy schoolchildren and later developed cancer before age 30 with 29 age-matched people who did not. The samples were taken an average of about nine years before diagnosis, and most positive samples were drawn six to 15 years earlier. The authors note that this window fits within the five to 20 years it is commonly thought to take for cancer to begin developing.
About 57% of those who later got cancer carried at least one of six core autoantibodies, compared with 14% of the comparison group. That made them about eight times as likely to carry these antibodies, although the statistical range was wide, from about 2.5 to 25 times, reflecting the small sample. Only one antibody, against UNG, was statistically significant on its own.
In laboratory tests, antibodies from both patients and healthy people entered living cells. However, patients' blood was far more likely to produce a distinct cloud-like pattern near the cell nucleus, and some DNA repair-related proteins, including RAD52, were found trapped in these clouds. The researchers suggest that this could interfere with DNA repair and allow mutations to build up, but they have not shown that it happens in the body.
Evidence Limits and a Patent Disclosure
Ola Myklebost, a professor of molecular oncology at the University of Bergen and the study's senior author, told Newsweek, "More work is required to prove causality."
An outside expert raised the same question. Dr. Yvonne Saenger, a cancer immunotherapy researcher who was not involved in the work, told Newsweek that the concept is interesting but that more research is needed to determine whether the antibodies develop in response to a tumor or predispose people to cancer.
The study was observational, combined with laboratory experiments in cell cultures; no animal or human trials were done. The pre-diagnosis group was small; about half of the British cases were older than 20 at diagnosis and had mostly adult-type cancers, and the first discovery group lacked child controls. The authors also say they cannot rule out that an early, undetected process leading to cancer triggers the antibodies.
The research was funded mainly by Norwegian cancer charities and research foundations, with the British cohorts supported by U.K. funders including Wellcome and the Medical Research Council. Lead author Anastassia Serguienko and Myklebost have filed a patent application to use the core autoantibodies as biomarkers.
What Comes Next
Through the University of Bergen's KidImmune project on autoimmunity in pediatric cancer, led by Myklebost, a grant from the Trond Mohn Research Foundation will fund testing of selected antibodies in much larger groups. The authors also say experiments in cancer-prone mice should be done to test whether specific antibodies can cause cancer-related damage.
Myklebost told Newsweek, "If everything holds, it could be possible to screen children for the presence of such antibodies to detect cancer risk." Getting there would require large studies showing that the antibodies reliably predict cancer without causing many false alarms.
What Parents Should Know Now
Parents do not need to seek an antibody test after this study. No approved test exists, and none is recommended for screening healthy children. In this research, some healthy children also carried these antibodies, so a positive result would not mean a child has or will develop cancer.
The most useful steps remain familiar ones: keep up with routine checkups, share family cancer history with your child's doctor, and call the doctor about symptoms that persist without explanation. The American Cancer Society lists possible signs of cancer in children such as ongoing fevers, easy bruising or bleeding, a new lump, unexplained weight loss, and bone pain. It also notes that these symptoms are much more likely to have causes other than cancer.
The most common childhood cancers are leukemias, brain and other central nervous system tumors, and lymphomas. Survival has improved greatly over the past half-century. Five-year survival for children and teens was above 85% in most age groups in 2013 to 2019, according to the National Cancer Institute, and 92.3% for children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2014 to 2020.
Key Questions Answered
What did the University of Bergen study find? People who later developed cancer were more likely to have carried autoantibodies against DNA repair proteins as healthy schoolchildren, on average about nine years before diagnosis.
Do these antibodies cause cancer? That has not been shown. The study found an association, and the authors say an early process leading to cancer could instead trigger the antibodies.
How many people were studied? The key pre-diagnosis analysis compared 30 people who later developed cancer with 29 who did not. The earlier analysis included 175 patients and 141 healthy people.
Can parents get their child tested for these antibodies? No. There is no approved or recommended test for screening healthy children.
Are there conflicts of interest? Lead author Anastassia Serguienko and senior author Ola Myklebost have filed a patent application to use the antibodies as biomarkers.
What symptoms should parents watch for? Call a doctor about unexplained symptoms that persist, such as ongoing fevers, easy bruising, a new lump, weight loss, or bone pain. Most have causes other than cancer.
